title: Option (finance)
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: An option is a contract that gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed price on or before a fixed date.
The fixed price is called the strike price and the fixed date is called the expiration date.
A call option gives the right to buy the underlying asset, and a put option gives the right to sell it.
The buyer of an option pays a premium to the seller, and the premium is the most the buyer can lose.
The seller of an option receives the premium and takes on the obligation to deliver or take delivery if the buyer exercises.
One listed equity option contract usually controls one hundred shares of the underlying stock.
An option is in the money when exercising it would be profitable at the current price, at the money when the strike equals the current price, and out of the money otherwise.
The value of an option has two parts, intrinsic value from being in the money and time value from the chance of moving further in the money before expiration.
Options are traded on exchanges such as the CBOE, where prices are quoted as a bid and an ask per share.

title: Call option
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
sentences: A call option is a contract that gives its holder the right to buy an underlying asset at the strike price on or before expiration.
A call gains value when the underlying price rises above the strike, because the holder can buy below the market.
The most a call buyer can lose is the premium paid, while the potential gain is unlimited as the underlying rises.
A call seller, also called a call writer, receives the premium and must sell the underlying at the strike if assigned.
A covered call is a call sold by someone who already owns the underlying shares, so assignment is funded by those shares.
The delta of a call is between zero and one, and it approaches one as the call moves deep in the money.
Calls are used to speculate on a rise, to hedge a short position, or to earn income by writing them against shares.

title: Put option
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
sentences: A put option is a contract that gives its holder the right to sell an underlying asset at the strike price on or before expiration.
A put gains value when the underlying price falls below the strike, because the holder can sell above the market.
The most a put buyer can lose is the premium paid, while the gain is capped at the strike price minus the premium.
A put seller receives the premium and must buy the underlying at the strike if assigned.
A cash-secured put is a put sold with enough cash set aside to buy the shares if assigned.
The delta of a put is between minus one and zero, and it approaches minus one as the put moves deep in the money.
Puts are used to hedge long positions, to speculate on a decline, or to earn income by writing them at prices where the seller is willing to buy.

title: Strike price
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: A strike price is a fixed price at which the holder of an option may buy or sell the underlying asset.
The strike is set when the contract is listed and does not change during the life of the option.
Exchanges list many strikes for each expiration, spaced by fixed intervals such as one dollar or five dollars.
The distance between the strike and the current underlying price determines whether an option is in, at, or out of the money.
Open interest tends to cluster at round-number strikes, which is why those strikes matter in dealer gamma analysis.
A strike with very large call open interest is often called a call wall, and a strike with very large put open interest a put wall.

title: Expiration date (options)
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: An expiration date is a fixed date after which an option contract can no longer be exercised and ceases to exist.
Days to expiration, abbreviated DTE, is the number of calendar days remaining until an option expires.
Listed equity options in the United States expire on Fridays, with weekly, monthly, and quarterly cycles, and the most active indexes expire every trading day.
An option with zero days to expiration is called a 0DTE option and expires at the close of that same session.
Time value decays toward zero as expiration approaches, and the decay accelerates in the final days.
At expiration an option is worth only its intrinsic value, so out-of-the-money options expire worthless.
Dealer gamma is concentrated in the nearest expirations, so the hedging effects that pin or accelerate price are strongest on expiration days.

title: Implied volatility
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
sentences: Implied volatility is a number, expressed as an annualized percentage, that makes a pricing model such as Black-Scholes reproduce the market price of an option.
Implied volatility is the market's forward-looking estimate of how much the underlying will move, in contrast to realized volatility, which measures how much it actually moved in the past.
A higher implied volatility means a higher option premium, because a larger expected range makes both calls and puts more likely to finish in the money.
Implied volatility usually rises when prices fall sharply and falls when prices grind higher, which is why the VIX index moves opposite to the stock market.
Different strikes on the same expiration carry different implied volatilities, and the pattern across strikes is called the volatility skew or smile.
The one standard deviation expected move of the underlying over a period is the price times the implied volatility times the square root of the fraction of a year in that period.
When dealers are short gamma, realized moves tend to exceed the implied move, and when they are long gamma realized moves tend to fall short of it.

title: Delta (options)
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
sentences: Delta is a number between minus one and one that gives the change in an option's price for a one-unit change in the price of the underlying.
A call has a delta between zero and one, and a put has a delta between minus one and zero.
Delta can be read as an approximate probability that the option finishes in the money, so a thirty-delta call has roughly a thirty percent chance of expiring in the money.
A position with total delta of zero is called delta neutral, and its value does not change for small moves in the underlying.
Delta hedging is the practice of buying or selling the underlying to keep a position delta neutral as prices change.
Market makers delta hedge the options they sell to customers, and the rebalancing of those hedges is the mechanism behind gamma exposure.
Delta itself changes as the underlying moves, and the rate of that change is gamma.

title: Gamma (options)
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
sentences: Gamma is a number that gives the change in an option's delta for a one-unit change in the price of the underlying.
Gamma is largest for at-the-money options near expiration and smallest for options that are far in or out of the money.
A position that gains delta as the underlying rises and loses delta as it falls is long gamma, and it profits from large moves in either direction.
A position that loses delta as the underlying rises and gains delta as it falls is short gamma, and it profits from calm markets but suffers from large moves.
A long gamma hedger sells the underlying as it rises and buys as it falls, which dampens price moves.
A short gamma hedger must buy the underlying as it rises and sell as it falls, which amplifies price moves.
Both calls and puts have positive gamma for the holder and negative gamma for the writer.
Dealer gamma exposure aggregates gamma across all open contracts to estimate whether the hedging flow will dampen or amplify the market.

title: Theta (options)
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
sentences: Theta is a number that gives the change in an option's price for the passage of one day with everything else unchanged.
Theta is negative for the holder of an option, because time value drains away as expiration approaches.
Theta is largest in magnitude for at-the-money options and accelerates in the final weeks before expiration.
Option sellers collect theta, which is why strategies such as the covered call, the cash-secured put, and the iron condor are called income strategies.
Time decay is the cost that a long option must overcome through a favorable move in price or volatility.
A scenario fan that reprices an option at later horizons charges theta at each step, so the same spot level is worth less the later it is reached.

title: Vega (options)
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
sentences: Vega is a number that gives the change in an option's price for a one percentage point change in implied volatility.
Vega is positive for the holder of a call or a put, because higher volatility raises the value of both.
Vega is largest for at-the-money options with a long time to expiration.
A long vega position profits when implied volatility rises, which usually happens in a sell-off, and loses when volatility is crushed after an event.

Volatility crush is the sharp drop in implied volatility after an earnings report or other scheduled event, and it can cause a long option to lose value even when the underlying moved in the expected direction.

title: Black-Scholes model
references: Fischer Black and Myron Scholes, The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities (1973)
Robert C. Merton, Theory of Rational Option Pricing (1973)
sentences: The Black-Scholes model is a mathematical model that gives the fair price of a European option from the underlying price, the strike, the time to expiration, the risk-free interest rate, and the volatility.
The model was published by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in 1973 and extended by Robert Merton in the same year.
Black-Scholes assumes that the underlying price follows a lognormal random walk with constant volatility and that trading is continuous with no transaction costs.
The formula prices a call as the underlying price times a probability term minus the discounted strike times a second probability term, where the probability terms come from the normal distribution.
The greeks delta, gamma, theta, and vega are the partial derivatives of the Black-Scholes price with respect to the underlying, the underlying again, time, and volatility.
Implied volatility is found by inverting the model, solving for the volatility that reproduces the market price.
Real markets violate the constant volatility assumption, which shows up as the volatility skew, but the model remains the common language for quoting and hedging options.

title: Gamma exposure
references: SqueezeMetrics, The Implied Order Book (2020)
Nomura and Goldman Sachs dealer positioning research notes
sentences: Gamma exposure is a measure of how much option dealers must buy or sell of the underlying to stay hedged for each one percent move in its price.
Gamma exposure is usually written GEX and is quoted in dollars per one percent move.
Per strike, gamma exposure is the option's gamma times open interest times one hundred shares times the underlying price squared times one percent.
The usual convention treats dealers as long the calls that customers sold and short the puts that customers bought, so call gamma counts positive and put gamma counts negative.
Net gamma exposure is the sum across all strikes and expirations, and its sign tells whether the hedging flow will dampen or amplify the market.
When net gamma exposure is positive, dealers sell into rallies and buy into dips, which suppresses volatility and tends to pin price near large strikes.
When net gamma exposure is negative, dealers buy strength and sell weakness, which amplifies moves and widens the daily range.

The level where net gamma exposure crosses zero is called the gamma flip, the strike with the largest positive exposure is the call wall, and the strike with the largest negative exposure is the put wall.
Gamma exposure is an estimate built from public open interest, not a record of actual dealer books, so it is a map of likely hedging pressure rather than a measurement of it.

title: Gamma flip
references: SqueezeMetrics, The Implied Order Book (2020)
sentences: A gamma flip is a price level of the underlying at which net dealer gamma exposure changes sign from positive to negative.
Above the gamma flip dealers are net long gamma and their hedging dampens moves, and below it they are net short gamma and their hedging amplifies moves.
The gamma flip is found by recomputing net gamma exposure at a range of hypothetical underlying prices and locating the crossing.
A market trading above its gamma flip tends to grind and mean revert, while a market that breaks below its flip tends to trend and expand in range.
The flip level moves as open interest changes and as expirations roll off, so it is recomputed from each new chain snapshot.
Traders use the gamma flip as a regime line, favoring premium-selling strategies above it and directional or long-volatility strategies below it.

title: Call wall
references: SqueezeMetrics, The Implied Order Book (2020)
sentences: A call wall is a strike price that carries the largest positive dealer gamma exposure in an option chain.
The call wall acts as a natural ceiling because dealers who are long gamma at that strike sell the underlying as price approaches it.
Price often stalls or reverses at the call wall, and a decisive break above it usually requires the wall to roll higher as new calls are opened.
The call wall is one of the three reference levels in a gamma exposure profile, together with the gamma flip and the put wall.
As expiration approaches, the gamma at the call wall grows, so its pinning effect is strongest on expiration day.

title: Put wall
references: SqueezeMetrics, The Implied Order Book (2020)
sentences: A put wall is a strike price that carries the largest negative dealer gamma exposure in an option chain.
The put wall acts as a support level because the hedging demand concentrated there tends to absorb selling as price approaches it.
A break below the put wall removes that support and often coincides with a move below the gamma flip, where hedging turns from dampening to amplifying.
The put wall is usually below the current price and marks where customers hold the most protective puts.
The put wall, the gamma flip, and the call wall together bracket the range that dealer hedging is expected to defend.

title: Dealer hedging
references: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
SqueezeMetrics, The Implied Order Book (2020)
sentences: Dealer hedging is a practice in which option market makers buy or sell the underlying asset to offset the delta of the options they have sold to customers.
A dealer who sells a call to a customer buys shares to hedge, and a dealer who sells a put sells shares or futures to hedge.
Because delta changes with price, dealers must rebalance their hedges continuously, and the direction of that rebalancing depends on the sign of their gamma.
Long gamma dealers rebalance against the trend, selling rallies and buying dips, which stabilizes price.
Short gamma dealers rebalance with the trend, buying rallies and selling dips, which destabilizes price.
Dealer hedging flow is mechanical and predictable from open interest, which is why gamma exposure models can anticipate where price will pin or accelerate.
Charm and vanna are second-order effects in which dealer hedges change with the passage of time and with implied volatility, producing flows near expiration and after volatility shifts.

title: Open interest
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: Open interest is a count of option contracts that have been opened and not yet closed, exercised, or expired.
Open interest rises when a new buyer and a new seller create a contract and falls when an existing position is closed.
Unlike volume, which counts trades during a day, open interest measures the standing size of positions at the end of the day.
Large open interest at a strike means that a large hedging position is attached to it, which is why gamma exposure weights each strike by open interest.
Open interest is published once daily by the exchange, so a gamma exposure profile computed from it is a daily map rather than a live one.

title: Covered call
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
sentences: A covered call is a strategy in which an investor owns shares of a stock and sells a call option against those shares.
The premium received lowers the cost basis of the shares and provides income while the stock is held.
If the stock finishes above the strike at expiration, the shares are called away at the strike and the upside beyond it is given up.
If the stock finishes below the strike, the call expires worthless, the premium is kept, and a new call can be sold.
A common covered call sells a thirty-delta call about thirty days out, which balances premium against the chance of being called away.
Covered calls outperform buy and hold in flat or gently rising markets and underperform in strong rallies.
The covered call is the second half of the wheel strategy, which begins with cash-secured puts.

title: Cash-secured put
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: A cash-secured put is a strategy in which an investor sells a put option while holding enough cash to buy the shares at the strike if assigned.
The premium received is kept whether or not the put is assigned.
If the stock finishes below the strike, the investor buys the shares at the strike, with an effective cost of the strike minus the premium.
If the stock finishes above the strike, the put expires worthless and a new put can be sold.
Selling a put at a strike where the investor is happy to own the stock turns a limit order into a paid limit order.
The cash-secured put is the first half of the wheel strategy.

title: Wheel strategy
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: The wheel strategy is a cycle in which an investor sells cash-secured puts until assigned shares, then sells covered calls on those shares until they are called away, and then begins again.
Each turn of the wheel collects a premium, so the strategy earns income in both phases.
The wheel works best on stocks the investor is willing to own for a long period, because assignment can leave the investor holding shares through a decline.
A typical wheel sells puts and calls at about thirty delta with thirty days to expiration.
The wheel underperforms buy and hold in strong rallies, because the covered call phase caps the upside, and it loses in sharp crashes, because assigned shares fall with the market.
A backtest of the wheel must model the option prices at each roll, and the HOODBarons backtester does this with Black-Scholes at a stated multiple of realized volatility.

title: Iron condor
references: Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
CBOE, The Options Institute
sentences: An iron condor is a four-legged option strategy that sells an out-of-the-money put and an out-of-the-money call while buying a further out-of-the-money put and call as wings.
The short strikes collect premium and the long wings cap the loss on each side.
The strategy profits when the underlying stays between the short strikes through expiration and loses when it breaks beyond either wing.
The maximum profit is the net credit received and the maximum loss is the width of a wing minus the credit.
Iron condors are placed by expected move, often at about one standard deviation, or by dealer gamma levels, with the short strikes at the put wall and the call wall.
Placing the short strikes at the walls uses the dealer hedging that defends those levels as an ally of the position.
Iron condors work best when net gamma exposure is positive and the market is pinned, and they are dangerous below the gamma flip where ranges expand.

title: Straddle (options)
references: Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
sentences: A straddle is a strategy that buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiration, usually at the money.
A long straddle profits from a large move in either direction and loses if the underlying stays near the strike while time decays.
The breakeven points of a straddle are the strike plus and minus the total premium paid.
A straddle is long gamma and long vega, so it gains from both movement and rising implied volatility.
A gamma flip straddle is a straddle bought when the underlying is about to cross the gamma flip, on the reasoning that dealer hedging will amplify the next move.
A short straddle sells both legs and profits from calm, and it is the position that market makers are typically carrying when net gamma exposure is positive.

title: Zero days to expiration
references: CBOE, The Options Institute
Nomura dealer positioning research notes
sentences: Zero days to expiration options are options that expire at the close of the same trading session in which they are traded.
0DTE options carry very high gamma and very fast theta, so their prices change rapidly with small moves in the underlying.
Index products such as SPX and SPY list expirations every trading day, which made 0DTE trading a large share of volume.
Because gamma is concentrated in the nearest expiration, 0DTE open interest dominates the intraday dealer hedging that pins or accelerates price.
A 0DTE pin fade is a strategy that sells premium at the call wall and put wall on expiration day, betting that dealer hedging holds price inside those levels into the close.
0DTE strategies require intraday chain data, so they cannot be backtested from daily snapshots alone.

title: Expected move
references: Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
sentences: The expected move is a price range that the option market implies the underlying will stay within about sixty-eight percent of the time over a given period.
The expected move equals the underlying price times the implied volatility times the square root of the period as a fraction of a year.
A quick estimate of the expected move to expiration is the price of the at-the-money straddle.
Traders compare the expected move to the distance to the call wall and the put wall to judge whether the dealer levels are reachable before expiration.
Realized moves exceed the expected move when dealers are short gamma and fall short of it when dealers are long gamma.

title: Backtesting
references: Ernest Chan, Quantitative Trading
Marcos Lopez de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning
sentences: Backtesting is a method that evaluates a trading strategy by applying its rules to historical market data and measuring the results.
A backtest reports metrics such as total return, compound annual growth rate, maximum drawdown, Sharpe ratio, and number of trades.
Every backtest is compared to buy and hold on the same asset over the same window, because a strategy that fails to beat the benchmark adds only risk.
Look-ahead bias is the error of using information in a backtest that would not have been available at the time of each decision.
Overfitting is the error of tuning a strategy so closely to one period of history that it fails on new data.
Cycling a strategy through many different windows, including bear markets and crashes, is the simplest defense against overfitting.
Option strategies are hard to backtest because historical chains are expensive, so a backtester either buys that data or models option prices from the underlying with a pricing model.
A modeled backtest should state its pricing assumptions plainly, because its credits and losses are estimates rather than fills.

title: Maximum drawdown
references: Ernest Chan, Quantitative Trading
sentences: Maximum drawdown is a measure of the largest decline from a peak to a subsequent trough in the value of a portfolio or strategy.
Drawdown is expressed as a negative percentage of the peak value.
A strategy with a fifty percent drawdown needs a one hundred percent gain to recover, so drawdown measures the pain of a strategy better than its average return.
Maximum drawdown is computed by tracking the running peak of the equity curve and recording the deepest fall below it.
Investors compare the maximum drawdown of a strategy to that of buy and hold to see whether the strategy reduces risk.

title: Sharpe ratio
references: William F. Sharpe, The Sharpe Ratio (1994)
sentences: The Sharpe ratio is a measure of the return of a strategy per unit of risk, computed as the average excess return divided by the standard deviation of returns.
The ratio was introduced by William Sharpe in 1966 and remains the most common single number for comparing strategies.
A Sharpe ratio above one is generally considered good for a strategy on daily data, and above two is rare over long periods.
Daily Sharpe ratios are annualized by multiplying by the square root of the number of trading days in a year, about two hundred fifty-two for stocks and three hundred sixty-five for crypto.
The Sharpe ratio penalizes upside volatility as much as downside volatility, so it can understate strategies with large positive skew.

title: Dollar-cost averaging
references: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor
sentences: Dollar-cost averaging is a strategy that invests a fixed amount of money at regular intervals regardless of the price of the asset.
Buying a fixed dollar amount purchases more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high, which lowers the average cost per unit compared to buying a fixed number of units.
Dollar-cost averaging reduces the risk of investing a lump sum right before a decline, at the cost of lower expected return when the market rises steadily.
The strategy is popular for crypto and index funds because it removes timing decisions.
In a backtest, dollar-cost averaging is compared to a lump-sum buy and hold over the same window to measure the price paid for the timing insurance.

title: Moving average crossover
references: Ernest Chan, Quantitative Trading
sentences: A moving average crossover is a trend-following strategy that buys when a fast moving average rises above a slow moving average and sells when it falls below.
A simple moving average is the mean of the closing prices over a fixed number of days.
The crossover of the fifty-day average above the two-hundred-day average is called a golden cross, and the reverse is called a death cross.
Crossover strategies capture long trends and avoid deep bear markets, but they lose money in choppy sideways markets through repeated false signals, called whipsaws.
Faster averages such as twenty and fifty days react sooner and whipsaw more, while slower averages react later and whipsaw less.

title: Mean reversion (finance)
references: Ernest Chan, Algorithmic Trading
sentences: Mean reversion is a tendency of a price to return toward its average after moving far from it.
A mean reversion strategy buys after a sharp decline and sells after the recovery, betting that the extreme will not persist.
The relative strength index, abbreviated RSI, is an oscillator between zero and one hundred that measures recent gains against recent losses, and a very low reading marks a washed-out condition.
A short RSI such as the two-day RSI below ten is a common buy signal for mean reversion in stock indexes.
Mean reversion works well in ranging markets and above the gamma flip, where dealer hedging dampens moves, and it fails in trending markets where the extreme keeps extending.
Mean reversion and momentum are opposite bets on the same price series, and which one works depends on the regime.

title: Momentum (finance)
references: Jegadeesh and Titman, Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers (1993)
sentences: Momentum is a tendency of assets that have risen recently to keep rising and of assets that have fallen recently to keep falling.
A momentum strategy buys recent winners and avoids or sells recent losers, holding for weeks to months.
Momentum was documented by Jegadeesh and Titman in 1993 and has been found in stocks, futures, currencies, and crypto.
Trend following is momentum applied to a single asset through rules such as the moving average crossover.
Momentum strategies suffer sharp reversals, called momentum crashes, when a trend breaks suddenly.
Momentum tends to work below the gamma flip, where dealer hedging amplifies moves, and to stall above it.

title: Cryptocurrency
references: Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008)
sentences: A cryptocurrency is a digital asset that is recorded on a public ledger called a blockchain and transferred without a central bank or intermediary.
Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first cryptocurrency, and Ethereum, launched in 2015, added programmable contracts to the model.
Cryptocurrencies trade twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, on exchanges such as Binance and Coinbase.
Crypto prices are far more volatile than stock indexes, with realized volatility that is often three to five times higher.
Crypto strategies are backtested on daily closes with the same tools as stocks, with the year counted as three hundred sixty-five trading days rather than two hundred fifty-two.
Options on Bitcoin and Ethereum trade on venues such as Deribit, and their dealer gamma follows the same mathematics as equity options.

title: Bitcoin
references: Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008)
sentences: Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency that was created in 2009 by a pseudonymous author known as Satoshi Nakamoto.
Bitcoin has a fixed supply cap of twenty-one million coins, issued on a schedule that halves roughly every four years.
Bitcoin is traded against the dollar and against stablecoins such as USDT on exchanges around the world.
Bitcoin's price history shows repeated cycles of large rallies followed by drawdowns of more than seventy percent.
Dollar-cost averaging and moving average crossovers are the most common simple strategies applied to Bitcoin, and both are available in the HOODBarons backtester.

title: Volatility skew
references: Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing
sentences: Volatility skew is a pattern in which options at different strikes on the same expiration trade at different implied volatilities.
In stock indexes, out-of-the-money puts carry higher implied volatility than out-of-the-money calls, because investors pay more for crash protection.
The skew is a market correction to the Black-Scholes assumption of constant volatility.
A steep skew makes put walls more expensive to build and reflects heavy demand for downside hedges.
Skew is measured as the difference in implied volatility between a put and a call of equal distance from the money.

title: Pinning (options)
references: Avellaneda and Lipkin, A Market-Induced Mechanism for Stock Pinning (2003)
sentences: Pinning is a tendency of an underlying price to close at or very near a strike with large open interest on expiration day.
Pinning is caused by dealer hedging, because long gamma dealers sell above the strike and buy below it, pushing price back toward it.
Avellaneda and Lipkin modeled pinning in 2003 as a market-induced effect of hedging flow near expiration.
Max pain is the strike at which the total value of expiring options is smallest, and it is often close to the pin.
Pinning is strongest when net gamma exposure is positive and weakest or absent when dealers are short gamma.

title: HOODBarons
references: Prometheus7, prometheus7.com/HOODBarons
sentences: HOODBarons is a finance strategy application built by Prometheus7 that screens dealer gamma exposure, prices option scenarios, and backtests strategies on real market history.
The application computes gamma exposure per strike from public open interest with Black-Scholes gamma and reports the gamma flip, the call wall, and the put wall.
The options check prices a chosen contract across the dealer levels and several time horizons under a stated implied volatility rule, as a scenario fan rather than a forecast.

The backtester runs built-in strategies such as buy and hold, dollar-cost averaging, moving average crossover, RSI mean reversion, covered calls, the wheel, and iron condors at the walls over daily history for stocks and crypto.
HOODBarons captures every chain it screens into its own options archive, so its option history grows daily instead of being purchased.
The explain layer of HOODBarons is a dedicated Oracle7 instance compiled from a finance corpus, which answers with references to that corpus.
HOODBarons is a tool for education and backtesting, it places no orders, links no accounts, and gives no investment advice.
